news.title: Nvidia's board reportedly prepares to oust Jensen Huang
news.summary: Reports say Nvidia's board is working with an outside firm on possible replacements for its founder-CEO as a second affair, with a senior Nvidia executive, came to light. Shares fell sharply after hours and are down about 20% since the scandal began.

news.title: Anthropic shuts off Claude access across mainland China
news.summary: An updated regional policy now bars use from mainland China, from companies registered there and from entities controlled from restricted regions. Accounts showing risk signals must verify identity or be closed.

news.title: DeepMind releases AlphaGenome 2 for research use
news.summary: The new DNA model, trained on more than 107 million cell profiles, flags nearly twice as many gene-expression-altering variants as the first version. It is available through an API for non-commercial research.

news.title: Gemini Robotics 2.5 posts 96% success in Mercedes-Benz parts trial
news.summary: DeepMind's new vision-language-action model improved task success across more than 200 tested activities. Apptronik reported 96% success packing auto parts, and the model is going to partners including Boston Dynamics.

news.title: Hackers used open-source AI agents to steal 2,000 Tajik government files
news.summary: CloudSEK says a Kazakhstan-linked group used the Hermes agent framework to plan the intrusion, write scripts and build a custom exfiltration tool. The operation surfaced only because the attackers left a server exposed.

news.title: CoreWeave turns to $9B in customer prepayments to fund growth
news.summary: The GPU cloud expects about $9 billion in prepayments and deposits over three months and is shifting to cheaper secured loans. It plans to add 500 MW of active power, reaching 1.5 GW.

news.title: US and China set first frontier-AI dialogue for APEC in Shenzhen
news.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two countries will talk about evaluating advanced models and alerting each other to serious incidents, while still competing. The first meeting is planned for the Nov 18–19 APEC summit.

news.title: Records show PLA-linked university bought Nvidia H200 chips
news.summary: Procurement documents show a Chinese university on the US Entity List bought H200s through a reseller with no known export license. Reuters found 26 similar records involving military-linked buyers.

news.title: EU sets common rules for AI Act regulatory sandboxes
news.summary: A new implementing regulation standardizes how member states create and supervise sandboxes where companies can test AI systems under regulators' watch. The aim is to avoid 27 different regimes.

news.title: Databricks launches always-on Genie agent
news.summary: The second-generation Genie runs in the background on its own compute, hands work to sub-agents and reports through a priority inbox and email. It connects to more than 100 enterprise data sources.

news.title: Microsoft Research backdoors AI agents by editing under 10 neurons
news.summary: The 'Lazarus' technique plants hidden behaviors by reprogramming a handful of dormant neurons, with no retraining. Frontier agents sometimes spot the tampering, but not reliably.

news.title: Spotify plans a $5-a-month AI remix add-on for 2027
news.summary: Universal, Merlin and Believe have signed on to let subscribers generate AI remixes and covers, while Sony and Warner are still negotiating. Artists will be able to opt out.

papers.title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Linking each stored lesson to the past run it came from lets AI agents check their memory, raising average scores from 87.0 to 90.2 while cutting how often memory breaks tasks they could already solve.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
WikiTrace gives AI agents a memory where every saved lesson links back to the original attempt it came from, so the agent can check a lesson before trusting it.

## Background you need
An LLM agent is a language model that acts step by step, for example in a text game or a set of apps. Many agents keep an external memory of lessons pulled from past tasks. A trajectory is the full record of one run: the model's reasoning, its actions and what it saw.

## The problem
Memory is supposed to help, but it can also hurt. The authors call this memory-induced degradation: the agent fails a task it would have solved with no memory at all. They measure it as Regression, the share of tasks that turn from success into failure once memory is added. Popular memory methods showed Regression as high as just rerunning the agent without memory. In these broken tasks, 52% of failures traced to a memory item the agent followed, most often a plainly wrong lesson. The root issue: lessons are stored without their source runs, so the agent cannot check them.

## The idea
Think of a wiki where every claim has a footnote. A careful reader usually trusts the text, but clicks the footnote when something looks odd. WikiTrace builds agent memory this way: short lessons, each pointing to a diagnosis of its run and to the untouched raw record.

## How it works
1. **Build three linked layers.** After each run, a compiler (another model call) diagnoses why it worked or failed. It then extracts up to three short insights: what to do, when, and whether the source run succeeded. The raw trajectory is kept unchanged.
2. **Never overwrite.** Insights are never edited or deleted, so the pool can hold contradictions the agent must sort out.
3. **Hand the agent its memory.** A new task starts with all insights, plus the three most similar past runs, stored as read-only files.
4. **Descend when in doubt.** If an insight lacks a needed detail, comes from a failed run, conflicts with another, or an action fails, the agent follows the links. It uses ordinary file-reading and terminal commands to find the exact fact, such as a command format, and may revise the insight before acting.

## Results
Tests covered five benchmarks (eight suites), from household text games to app-using tasks. Averaged over all eight, the agent scored 79.5 with no memory. Existing memory methods scored between 80.3 and 81.7. The same insights without links scored 87.0, and WikiTrace scored 90.2. It was best on every suite and the only method never below the no-memory agent. Regression fell to 4.5%, versus 6.5% for insights alone and 9.7% for a plain rerun. So about one in twenty solvable tasks broke, not one in ten. The agent looked up sources in 22% of easy tasks and 44% of hard ones. Opening a source changed the plan in 43% of those runs. The extra lookups cost about 1.17 times as much per task as insights alone. Gains held with a second model family.

## Why it matters
Assistants that learn from experience risk silent regressions, where yesterday's lesson breaks today's task. Keeping evidence next to each lesson is a cheap pattern to copy, and it makes memory easier to audit.

## Caveats
Lessons still come from simple pass/fail labels, so diagnoses can be wrong; a link lets the agent check a lesson but does not prove it. All insights go into the opening prompt, which will not scale to very large memories. The failure causes were labeled by a model reading the agent's stated reasoning, not by verified analysis. Most experiments used one agent model.

## Key terms
- **LLM agent**: a language model that takes actions step by step to finish a task.
- **Trajectory**: the full record of one attempt, including reasoning, actions and observations.
- **Memory-induced degradation**: failing a task because of memory that would have been solved without it.
- **Regression**: the share of previously solved tasks that memory turns into failures.
- **Descent**: the agent following a lesson's links down to its original evidence.

papers.title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: An agent loop guided by a cost model finds and verifies optimizations for speculative decoding, raising single-request speedup from 4.46x to 10.87x and batched speedup from 1.94x to 3.93x with no training or quality loss.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
SpecPilot lets AI coding agents tune an existing text-generation speedup system on their own, more than doubling the speedup it delivered.

## Background you need
A large language model writes text one small piece at a time, and each piece is called a token. Speculative decoding speeds this up. A small "drafter" model guesses several upcoming tokens, and the big "target" model checks all of the guesses in one pass. A parallel drafter guesses a whole block of tokens at once instead of one by one.

## The problem
Published speculative decoding systems rarely reach the speed their design allows, for three reasons. First, with one user at a time, each step accepts only a few drafted tokens. Most of the step goes to reading the model's weights (its learned numbers) from GPU memory, about 80% of step time by their profiling. Second, batching (serving many users together) roughly halves the advantage over normal decoding. Third, the best settings change with the model, the drafter and the GPU, so hand-tuning one setup does not carry over.

## The idea
Treat performance tuning as a search that AI agents can run, with strict rules about what counts as a real win. Think of a pit crew that fixes the slowest part of a race car first. It keeps a change only if the car is faster on a fresh track and a referee confirms it still follows the rules. Proven tricks go into a notebook for the next car.

## How it works
1. **Find the biggest gap.** A cost model splits each step's time into parts. The part furthest from its hardware limit (the fastest it could physically run) becomes the next target.
2. **Try fixes in parallel.** Several agents, each on its own GPU, write and test candidate changes.
3. **Accept only honest wins.** A controller keeps a change only if it stays faster on unseen requests. "Token forcing" checks every output token against the original system. This catches reward hacking, where an agent fakes a win by quietly changing the answers.
4. **Remember what worked.** Proven changes go into a memory, which held 140 verified entries in the paper. New setups can reuse them, after re-tuning and re-measuring.

Discoveries include a lossless 12-bit weight format that stores weights in fewer bits but restores them exactly. Others verify a tree of drafts instead of one chain, pre-check drafts with a cheap low-precision pass, and share the checking budget across batched users.

## Results
Without any training or loss of output quality, the single-user speedup over normal decoding rose from 4.46× to 10.87×. In practice, a reply that took 10.9 seconds with plain decoding and 2.4 seconds with the original system now takes about 1 second. With batching, the speedup rose from 1.94× to 3.93×. Tests covered four target models, three drafters, two GPU types and five benchmarks.

## Why it matters
Faster generation means cheaper serving and quicker replies for chatbots and coding assistants. More broadly, the work shows that AI agents can do careful systems tuning when checks stop them from cheating.

## Caveats
Batched gains are much smaller than single-user gains, and batching is how most real services run. The tricks do not transfer evenly across models, drafters or GPU generations. The search itself takes GPU time and engineering setup. This summary is based on the abstract and detailed third-party write-ups, since the full paper text could not be fetched.

## Key terms
- **Token:** a small chunk of text, often part of a word, that the model outputs one at a time.
- **Speculative decoding:** a small model guesses ahead and the big model checks the guesses in bulk.
- **Drafter / target:** the fast guessing model and the large model whose answers must be matched.
- **Batching:** serving many users' requests together on the same hardware.
- **Reward hacking:** gaming the score, such as looking faster by quietly changing outputs.

papers.title: Fast and Exact Relative-Position Attention via Structure-Aware Kernels
papers.tldr: New Triton GPU kernels compute relative-position attention exactly with up to 21x faster training passes and up to 128x less memory, letting speech and text models handle much longer inputs.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The authors wrote new GPU code that computes "distance-aware" attention exactly, but much faster and with far less memory, so existing models can handle long inputs like 20-minute recordings.

## Background you need
In attention, every token (a word piece or a slice of audio) looks at every other token and decides how much each matters. Many models also tell attention how far apart two tokens are; this is relative-position attention, used in speech recognizers and text models like DeBERTa. FlashAttention is a well-known trick that computes attention in small tiles inside the GPU's fast on-chip memory, instead of writing a huge table to slow main memory.

## The problem
FlashAttention only handles plain attention. Relative-position models add a "distance bonus" to every token pair. Most code builds that bonus as a full table: for 8,000 tokens, 64 million entries per attention head, stored in slow memory. That brings back the bottleneck FlashAttention removed. During training, many parallel workers also queue to update the same memory slots.

## The idea
The distance bonus is highly structured. Two tokens 5 apart get the same bonus wherever they sit, and past a cutoff all far pairs share one capped value. Think of a postal rate chart: you need a price per distance band, not per pair of towns, and beyond 500 km it is one flat rate. The new code reads the chart once per tile and reuses it.

## How it works
1. **One recipe.** Four well-known schemes (Shaw, Transformer-XL, DeBERTa and T5) are written as one formula. Each score gets at most three small add-on numbers based on distance.
2. **Only compute what is reachable.** Queries are handled in small groups, and each group prepares only the distance entries it can reach. This roughly halves that work for long inputs.
3. **Reuse flat regions.** Tiles far from the diagonal all share the capped value, so they load one entry and reuse it.
4. **No queuing in training.** In the backward pass (where the model works out how to adjust its weights), each tile has one writer that sums updates by distance. This avoids slow "atomic" additions and makes results deterministic.
5. **Drop-in code.** It is written in Triton, a GPU programming language, with adapters for popular toolkits.

## Results
On an NVIDIA H200 GPU, outputs always matched a high-precision reference. At 8,000 tokens, versus the best existing system per scheme, the forward pass was 1.8 to 6.4 times faster and the backward pass 2.0 to 21 times faster. Peak memory dropped up to 128 times. Transformer-XL gained less, 1.4 to 2.4 times. Every existing system failed the accuracy check on DeBERTa's backward pass from 4,000 tokens.

Real models gained too. Transcribing talks of up to 25 minutes with the Parakeet speech model, speed rose from 613 to 1,103 times real time versus PyTorch's built-in attention. Memory fell from 27 to 11 gigabytes, with similar error rates. When fine-tuning the Canary speech model, built-in attention ran out of memory at 15-minute clips; the new code trained on 18-minute clips. For DeBERTa on 4,000-token patents, training steps were 2.39 times faster and memory fell from 27 to 7.1 gigabytes, with accuracy within 0.3 points.

## Why it matters
Many production speech and text models already use relative positions. This lets them process long inputs without retraining or changing outputs. Speech teams could fine-tune on whole meetings.

## Caveats
Transformer-XL needs a separate entry per distance, so its work still grows with the square of length. Unusual schemes fall back to slower, non-deterministic updates, though none of the tested ones do. On very short inputs, T5's backward pass was slightly slower than existing tools. End-to-end gains are capped by attention's share of total time.

## Key terms
- **Relative-position attention:** attention that adds a bonus based on how far apart two tokens are.
- **Tiling:** splitting a big computation into blocks that fit in fast on-chip memory.
- **Backward pass:** the training step that computes how to adjust weights.
- **Atomic addition:** a safe but slow way for many workers to add into one memory slot.
- **Real-time factor:** seconds of audio processed per second of compute.

papers.title: HIERA: Workload-Aware Planning Across Implementation Spaces for GPU Kernel Optimization
papers.tldr: An LLM agent system that first decides whether a GPU task should use PyTorch operators, NVIDIA libraries, or custom CUDA, then refines step by step, beating other untrained agents on KernelBench.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
HIERA is a team of AI agents that writes fast GPU code. Before it writes anything, it decides how low-level that code should be for the job at hand.

## Background you need
A GPU kernel is a small program that runs one operation, such as a matrix multiply, across thousands of GPU cores at once. Kernels can be built at different levels. You can chain ready-made PyTorch operators (building blocks from a popular machine-learning library), call NVIDIA's tuned CUDA libraries, or write raw CUDA code yourself. KernelBench is a public test suite of 250 such tasks, split into three levels of growing complexity.

## The problem
Hand-writing fast kernels is slow expert work, and vendor libraries miss unusual workloads. Recent systems ask a large language model (an LLM, a text-generating AI) to write kernels instead. Most lock in one level up front. High-level-only systems miss tricks like fusing steps together. Raw-CUDA-only systems face a huge search space, and many attempts fail to compile, give wrong answers, or run no faster. Feedback polishes code within a level but never questions the level itself.

## The idea
Think of a kitchen contractor. Sometimes a stock cabinet is best; sometimes custom-built is worth it. A good contractor decides that first. HIERA plans the same way: pick the level per workload, pick one focused optimization direction, then write code.

## How it works
1. **Fixed contract.** Glue code and the correctness reference are supplied and frozen. The LLM writes only one CUDA file, which cuts boilerplate mistakes.
2. **Choose the level.** A planning agent picks one of three nested spaces: pure CUDA, CUDA plus vendor libraries, or libraries plus PyTorch operators.
3. **Choose a direction.** The agent then scores five kinds of optimization: control flow, thread parallelism, memory access, data reuse, and use of Tensor Cores (special matrix-math units). The top one wins.
4. **Plan and write.** A strategy agent makes a concrete plan; a coding agent writes candidate kernels.
5. **Test and repeat.** Candidates are compiled, checked, timed, and profiled with Nsight Compute (NVIDIA's tool showing where time is wasted). The best seed the next round.

## Results
Tests used an NVIDIA A100 GPU and all 250 KernelBench tasks. HIERA was compared with KernelBench's own iterative workflow, CUDAForge (another agent system), and CUDA-L1 (a model specially trained for this job). With 18 attempts per task, HIERA produced a working kernel for 92.4% of tasks and beat the reference speed on 60.4%. The two agent baselines beat the reference on only 29.6% and 44.8%. With the Qwen3.6-Plus model, it beat the reference on 68%, 62% and 42% of tasks at Levels 1–3. CUDAForge scored 47%, 45% and 40% with the same model. The trained CUDA-L1 still led on Level 3, at 50%.

Planning matters. Writing pure CUDA every time gave a median speedup of 0.62×, meaning the typical kernel was slower than the original. HIERA's choice of level gave a median of 1.15× and a mean of 1.42×. Removing the planner cut Level 2 wins from 62% to 6%. Removing contracts mainly hurt validity.

In a case study on an image-filter-style stencil (each output point averages a 7×7 neighborhood), the fifth round ran in 4.71 ms. NVIDIA's cuDNN library took 7.23 ms, so HIERA was 1.53× faster.

## Why it matters
Teams needing kernels for new model layers could get decent ones without a GPU specialist. The bigger lesson: the code level is itself worth searching over. It needs no model training, so off-the-shelf LLMs work.

## Caveats
Only A100 GPUs were tested; other chips, multi-GPU setups and low-precision formats were not. LLM output is random, so results vary between runs. The stencil win covers one operator and one input size.

## Key terms
- **Kernel:** a small GPU program that performs one operation in parallel.
- **CUDA:** NVIDIA's language for programming its GPUs directly.
- **Implementation space:** the level code is built at, from high-level library calls down to raw CUDA.
- **Speedup:** the old running time divided by the new one; above 1× means faster.
- **Stencil:** an operation where each output point is computed from its nearby input points.

papers.title: Learning Heterogeneous Tactile Representation for General Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: LingBot-Touch learns one shared touch representation from nearly 5,000 hours of data across three sensor types, and adding it to robot control models raised real-world task success by roughly 14 to 25 points.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
LingBot-Touch is one shared "touch encoder" for robot hands that reads three very different kinds of touch sensors and helps robot control models handle objects more reliably.

## Background you need
Many robot hands have touch sensors on their fingertips, like skin. Common types are piezoresistive (material whose resistance changes when pressed), magnetic (tiny magnets whose field shifts under pressure) and visuotactile (a small camera watching a soft pad deform). An encoder is a neural network that compresses raw readings into compact features other models can use.

## The problem
Vision and language models scaled because everyone shares one input format, like pixels or text. Touch has nothing similar. Each sensor reports different channels, layouts and speeds. So teams train custom models for one sensor on one hand, and they do not carry over. Adding raw touch data to a robot policy (the model that picks its next movements) often helps little, and in this paper's tests sometimes hurt.

## The idea
Touch readings depend on sensor physics, but the contact itself does not. A finger pressing a cup's rim is the same event whatever records it. Think of a translator who hears many accents but writes everything in one standard spelling. LingBot-Touch strips away each sensor's quirks and maps all readings into one common "fingertip space."

## How it works
1. **Build a large corpus.** The team gathered 4,983 hours of touch recordings, about 1.33 billion frames across 24 task categories. About two-thirds came from people wearing sensor gloves; the rest from remotely operated robot fingertips.
2. **Put every sensor on one map.** Each sensing point (a "taxel," like a touch pixel) gets a position in a shared fingertip frame, plus its time step and finger. Readings are scaled by each sensor's own range.
3. **Small front ends, one shared core.** Each sensor type gets a tiny input network that turns short snippets into tokens. All tokens feed one shared 12-layer Transformer, the network type behind chatbots.
4. **Train by predicting hidden parts.** The model hides up to 80% of the signal and predicts a compressed summary of the missing part, not raw values. This forces it to learn contact, not noise. Sensor layouts are also randomly thinned and jiggled so it never relies on one exact layout.
5. **Plug it into policies.** The trained encoder is frozen, and its tokens are added to existing control models. This adds only 0.13–0.16% more parameters.

## Results
On a hand seen in training, fingertip force error was 0.81 newtons versus 2.31 for an earlier touch model, FTP-1. On a magnetic hand never seen in training, it was 1.32 versus 3.72.

On 26 real-robot tasks, 20 trials each, touch tokens helped every policy type. A diffusion policy went from 21.6% to 35.6% success. The vision-language-action model π0.5 rose from 48.1% to 69.9%, and LingBot-VLA from 48.3% to 73.1%. Raw touch added at most about 11 points and hurt in 22 of 104 task-policy pairs. Across 12 simulated tasks, average success was 69.0%, versus 38.5% with raw touch and 21.4% with none.

## Why it matters
Robot builders could reuse one pretrained touch encoder instead of training one per sensor. More data kept helping: real-robot success climbed from 69.8% to 82.2% as pretraining grew from 1,000 to 5,000 hours. That hints touch may scale the way vision did.

## Caveats
Only a few hand designs were tested. Capacitive sensors were left out because available data was too poor. The model focuses on fingertips, so palm contact is underrepresented. With a fixed data budget, mixing sensors usually did slightly worse than one sensor alone. Precision on unseen sensors is lower, and simulated force estimates remain rough.

## Key terms
- **Taxel:** one touch-sensing point, like a pixel of a touch "image."
- **Tactile encoder:** a network turning raw touch readings into compact, useful features.
- **Policy:** the model that chooses a robot's next movements.
- **Vision-language-action model:** a large model mapping camera images and instructions to robot actions.
- **Latent prediction:** learning by guessing a compressed summary of hidden data rather than the data itself.

papers.title: Reframe: Observation-Aligned Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Visual Reasoning
papers.tldr: Reframe merges an image specialist and a video specialist into one tool-using vision-language model, correcting the student's bad crops or frame picks during training so it learns to rely on what its tools show it.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
Reframe trains one vision-language model to zoom into images and pick video frames with tools, and to actually use what it sees, by merging two specialist teachers and fixing the student's bad tool calls.

## Background you need
A vision-language model reads images or video plus text and answers questions about them. "Agentic" models can also call tools while reasoning, such as cropping part of a picture or selecting a few video frames to look at more closely. Reinforcement learning (trial and reward) and distillation (a student copying a stronger teacher) are the usual ways to teach this.

## The problem
There are two failures. First, models often call a tool and then ignore the result, answering as if they never looked. Second, one model that handles both images and video tends to do worse than separate image-only and video-only models. Existing methods that blend several teachers into one student only judge the student's words. If the student cropped the wrong region, the teacher is grading reasoning built on a useless view.

## The idea
Picture a photography student with two mentors, one for photos and one for film. If the student aims at the wrong spot, a good mentor doesn't just critique the caption. They move the camera and say "continue from here." Reframe does this: it treats what the model *sees* after a tool call as something to correct, not just what it *says*.

## How it works
1. **Build clean training data.** The authors assemble Reframe-100K, about 63,000 image questions and 37,000 video questions. Each comes labeled with the correct region or frames.
2. **Train two specialists.** Starting from Qwen3.5-9B, they train an image specialist (with a crop tool) and a video specialist (with a frame-selection tool). Rewards cover a correct answer, plus how well the chosen crop or frames overlap the labeled evidence.
3. **Hide the original picture sometimes.** After the first successful tool call, the original image or video is removed half the time. The model must then rely on what the tool returned.
4. **Merge with repaired observations.** A single student model generates answers, and the matching specialist grades each step. If the student's tool call misses the labeled evidence by too much, it is swapped for the correct call. The student continues from that better view and is also trained to make the corrected call itself.

## Results
Across 14 benchmarks (7 image, 7 video), Reframe averaged 69.48 on image tasks and 53.10 on video tasks. The base Qwen3.5-9B scored 63.46 and 49.75. Plain multi-teacher distillation scored 68.19 and 52.32. One model trained on mixed data with reinforcement learning scored 66.75 and 51.41. Reframe also beat both specialists on their own turf on average.

The largest single jump was on VisualProbe: 57.48 versus 52.62 for plain distillation. Tools helped Reframe by 5.23 points on image tasks; for the older agents DeepEyes, Thyme and Pixel-Reasoner, tools helped by under 1.5 points. On V*, handing Reframe the correct crop raised accuracy to 96.86, against 85.86 with a random crop. So the model really reads its tool output.

## Why it matters
Assistants that answer questions about screenshots, documents or long videos must zoom in on small details. A model that genuinely uses what it looked at is more reliable. The recipe skips a separate supervised warm-up stage, and the data, code and model are released.

## Caveats
Only one base model and two simple tools were tested. The method depends on good evidence labels; bad boxes or frame ranges would mislead both the rewards and the repairs. The "does it use the tool output" analysis covers just 191 questions. Swapped-in actions also mean the student partly learns from histories it did not write.

## Key terms
- **Tool call**: the model pausing to run an action, like cropping an image, and reading the result.
- **On-policy distillation**: a teacher grades text the student itself generated, rather than the student copying teacher-written examples.
- **Specialist teacher**: a model trained on only images or only video.
- **Overlap score**: how much a chosen crop or frame range matches the labeled correct one.
- **Tool gain**: accuracy with tools minus accuracy without them.
